title: Recording abroad with cheaper orchestras
summary: American stars record in London cheaply while US musicians are restricted.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: Sure. How do you feel about this, Jimmy? I know a lot of American artists------------ I just remember one very famous lady, done so many Broadway shows and she's quite a star, and we were there --
This lady was telling me, after this television show

she says, 'I'm going to London and I'm going to record, make an album of the songs from some of the Broadway shows I did. And I'm going to have 80 musicians in the band.' Well, she could get 80 musicians in London for what she could get eight for over here.

It made me feel very badly. And this lady was boasting, she didn't know how I felt about it. But here, when she's doing the television show, she's made her name and her reputation here with American songs, which American public had paid to see and American writers had written these songs, and she's going to go to England and record these songs. And the people in England didn't know her as well as the people over here. So the songs on this album will have to sell better over here. And (inaudible) here. How do you feel about that?

Well, I think it's pretty rough. I have a friend who has a record company. Now, he got a standard letter from the Philharmonia Symphony in London, and all these orchestras send out letters to American record companies and to ad agencies saying, you can have any size orchestra you want, 60 pieces, 70 pieces, $15.00 a man and no quibbling about overtime or anything else, and our top musicians.
Now, you remember there's a time when the agencies were going over there because they could put it on the expense
account, they'd take this girlfriend or the secretary along and it was cheaper to go over there, and they could get a small symphony for what they paid us.
And one of the things that I thought was rotten about that is that American musicians cannot go to England/ -- at that time, I don't know if they can now.
They can go as a single, but as a group you don't get to go.

Very strict laws restricting American musicians. And yet I think that American artists who make their reputation here with American musicians -- well, I say it's not fair from a moral point of view, but it's economics, I guess, and there's no such thing as a moral point of view in economics. You get into big enough money and you don't.
Except -- it's true. Except I don't think we have the expertise to know how to -- to educate the public to be aware that this is what's happening to American musicians.
